Product case study · Public summary

Understanding the query to invest in the right customer moment

A search query is more than a string of words. Classifying its intent can change how a retailer bids, which experience a customer sees, and where advertising investment creates the most value.

My contributionQuery-cohort strategy, multilingual classification product direction, measurement, and reinvestment of advertising spend.

The problem

Customer searches can be longer and more specific than a simple brand or product name. Yet a single advertising strategy can treat very different queries as if they have the same value. Branded, semi-branded, and generic searches may differ sharply in bid price, efficiency, and the customer experience they deserve.

The product question was: Can we understand the query well enough to spend less where clicks can be acquired efficiently, then redirect that capacity to cohorts and experiences where it matters more? At large scale, small differences in the cost of a click can meaningfully change the allocation of a budget.

Branded

The query names a brand or product explicitly. Strategy should account for strong existing intent and avoid overpaying for demand that is already close to purchase.

Semi-branded

The query mixes some brand context with broader exploration. It needs a strategy that reflects both known preference and remaining discovery.

Generic

The query expresses a category, use case, or need without a named brand. Relevance and customer guidance can matter more than brand recognition.

These cohort descriptions are simplified for a public reader. The production classification and bidding rules are not disclosed here.

The product strategy

I organized the work around three connected decisions: classify each query, set a distinct go-to-market and investment approach for each cohort, and use the resulting signal to improve the customer experience. The goal was not merely a better label. It was a better allocation of spend and a better match between the query and what the customer sees.

01 / Classify

Understand intent

Group queries into branded, semi-branded, and generic cohorts across the languages and markets in scope.

02 / Allocate

Price each opportunity

Use cohort-level efficiency and bid-clearance behavior to avoid paying more for a click than necessary, then redirect spend toward higher-value opportunities.

03 / Experience

Match the response

Let query intent inform the customer journey, so the landing experience and advertising approach fit the stage of discovery.

What changed

The classification and cohort strategy let us move investment toward the right opportunities while maintaining click volume more efficiently. It also gave teams a clearer way to reason about the experience shown for each type of query.

5%

of store-level advertising spend was repurposed toward the right query cohorts and strategies. The value came from reducing unnecessary spend for comparable click volume and reinvesting the capacity more deliberately. This is an allocation result, not a claim that total spend or customer demand fell by 5%.

How the classification evolved

The technical product work began with grounded, labeled query data and a Qwen-based model adapted for the languages in which the business operated. Fine-tuning improved the classifier substantially. We then used continued learning from an LLM to improve the fine-tuned model as language and query patterns changed.

This sequence mattered because a fixed training sample can age quickly. New phrasing and longer searches create cases that the original sample may not represent well. We tracked classification quality through F1: are queries being assigned to the right cohort while relevant queries are still found?

Starting point

~30% F1

Early performance showed that the initial approach did not yet classify the cohorts reliably enough.

Grounded fine-tuning

~85% F1

Fine-tuning on grounded examples created a much stronger multilingual classifier.

Continued LLM-based learning

~93–94% F1

Ongoing learning improved the model further as new query patterns emerged.

What F1 means: It balances precision (how many assigned labels are correct) with recall (how many relevant queries are found). Higher is better, but it is a model-quality measure, not by itself a business outcome. The figures above are approximate project milestones. See the technical definition of F1.

What I learned

The business value of query understanding depends on connecting model quality to decisions. A classifier can score well in isolation and still fail to change bidding, budget allocation, or the customer experience. This project linked the taxonomy, the model evaluation, and the go-to-market strategy into one product loop.

The multilingual language-understanding work also informed semantic matching and ranking in a separate trend-based advertising project. We published the grounded fine-tuning and continued-learning approach as a machine-learning conference case study. I can add a formal citation once the exact title and link are available.
